items.followUp: Give five differences between elements and compounds.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition and formula, while a mixture can have variable composition and no fixed formula.
rubric.description: States two valid composition or formula differences between compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for two correct differences; 1 mark if only one is given. Do not award twice for restating the same difference.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; a mixture’s components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of a compound and a mixture’s components.
rubric.how: Award for a correct comparison showing that the compound’s properties differ or the mixture’s components retain theirs.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated by chemical means, whereas mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the methods used to separate compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award for identifying chemical separation of compounds and physical separation of mixtures.

rubric.why: Compounds have definite melting and boiling points; mixtures generally do not.
rubric.description: Compares melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for stating the definite points of compounds and the lack of definite points in mixtures.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition and a definite formula; a mixture has variable composition and no definite formula.
A compound’s properties differ from those of its constituent elements; components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A compound has definite melting and boiling points; a mixture generally does not.
A compound is a pure substance, whereas a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

items.followUp: Write four physical properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.description: Gives the low melting or boiling points of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either or both low melting and boiling points.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity because they lack mobile charged particles.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds are poor conductors of electricity.
rubric.how: Award for identifying their lack of electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: They are generally insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.description: Gives the characteristic solubility of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award for the correct water/organic-solvent solubility comparison.

rubric.why: Many covalent compounds are gases or liquids; solid covalent compounds are often soft.
rubric.description: States their usual physical state or softness.
rubric.how: Award for identifying gases, liquids, or soft solids as typical covalent compounds.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
Many are gases or liquids; those that are solids are often soft.

items.followUp: Describe how cathode rays are produced and state two of their properties.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure when a high potential difference is applied between the electrodes.
rubric.description: Explains the conditions and direction involved in producing cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award for describing a low-pressure discharge tube with a high potential difference, or rays emerging from the cathode toward the anode.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines and can cast sharp shadows.
rubric.description: Gives two related observations showing rectilinear travel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for straight-line travel and 1 mark for producing a shadow; do not award more than 2 marks.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are negatively charged and are deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
rubric.description: States their negative charge and field deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for negative charge and 1 mark for deflection by an electric or magnetic field.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure when a high potential difference is applied between its electrodes.
They originate at the cathode and travel toward the anode.
Cathode rays travel in straight lines and can cast sharp shadows.
They carry a negative charge and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain materials.

items.followUp: Compare solutions and suspensions using particle size, appearance, and light scattering.

rubric.why: A solution is homogeneous; a colloid is heterogeneous, although it may appear homogeneous.
rubric.description: Compares the nature or appearance of solutions and colloids.
rubric.how: Award for correctly distinguishing a homogeneous solution from a colloid that is heterogeneous or appears homogeneous.

rubric.why: Solution particles are smaller than colloidal particles; solution particles are below 1 nm and colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm.
rubric.description: Compares the particle sizes.
rubric.how: Award for giving the correct relative sizes or the standard size ranges.

rubric.why: Solutions do not scatter light, while colloids show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.description: Compares light scattering.
rubric.how: Award for correctly contrasting no scattering in solutions with light scattering in colloids.

rubric.why: Particles of both pass through ordinary filter paper; colloidal particles cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.
rubric.description: Compares their behaviour during filtration.
rubric.how: Award for stating that colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper or are not separated by ordinary filtration, in contrast to solution particles also passing through.

modelAnswer: A solution is homogeneous; a colloid is heterogeneous but may appear homogeneous.
Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm; colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.
A solution does not scatter light; a colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect.
Particles of both pass through ordinary filter paper; colloidal particles are not separated by ordinary filtration.

items.followUp: Define relative atomic mass and state why it is used instead of the actual mass of an atom.

rubric.why: One atomic mass unit is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines the atomic mass unit using carbon-12.
rubric.how: Award for giving the one-twelfth-of-carbon-12 definition.

rubric.why: Atomic masses are extremely small, so the unit provides a convenient way to express and compare them.
rubric.description: Explains why the atomic mass unit is needed.
rubric.how: Award for stating that actual atomic masses are tiny or inconvenient and that the unit makes them easier to express or compare.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (amu) is one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
It is needed because the actual masses of atoms are extremely small and inconvenient to express; amu provides a convenient scale for comparing them.

items.followUp: Explain how electrons and positive ions form in a discharge tube.

rubric.why: Electrons from the cathode collide with gas atoms and ionise them, producing positive ions.
rubric.description: Explains the formation of positive ions in the tube.
rubric.how: Award for stating that gas atoms are ionised, for example by electron collisions.

rubric.why: Positive ions move toward the cathode and pass through holes in it, forming canal rays.
rubric.description: Explains how canal rays emerge through the cathode.
rubric.how: Award for stating that positive ions pass through the perforated cathode and form canal rays.

modelAnswer: Electrons emitted by the cathode collide with gas atoms in the discharge tube and ionise them, producing positive ions.
These positive ions move toward the cathode and pass through its perforations, producing canal rays.

items.followUp: State why Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability.

rubric.why: According to classical theory, revolving electrons should continuously radiate energy.
rubric.description: Identifies the energy-radiation problem for orbiting electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that orbiting electrons should radiate or lose energy.

rubric.why: The electrons should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would be unstable, contrary to observation.
rubric.description: States the predicted collapse and resulting failure to explain stability.
rubric.how: Award for stating that electrons should spiral or fall into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain why an atom is stable.
An electron revolving around the nucleus should continuously radiate energy and lose it.
It should therefore spiral into the nucleus, causing the atom to collapse.

items.followUp: State the rule used to form a Dobereiner triad and give one example.

rubric.why: A Dobereiner triad is a group of three elements with similar chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a Dobereiner triad.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it consists of three elements with similar properties.

rubric.why: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two.
rubric.description: States the atomic-mass relationship in a triad.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the middle element’s atomic mass as approximately the average of the other two.

modelAnswer: A Dobereiner triad is a group of three elements with similar chemical properties.
The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.
